en.title: Geology: the whole course
en.short: What geology covers, how geology degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What geology is
sections.text:
Geology is the study of the Earth: its materials, the processes that form and change them, its history, and its place in the solar system. It asks how rocks, minerals, fossils, water and landscapes come to be as they are, and how they change over time. It draws on physics, chemistry, biology and mathematics, but its central skill is careful observation in the field and the laboratory.

Geology matters because it helps societies find and manage water, minerals and energy, understand hazards such as earthquakes, landslides and volcanic eruptions, and assess ground for engineering works. It also informs environmental decisions about mining, waste and land use. A geology course therefore trains both scientific understanding and practical judgement.

sections.heading: How a geology degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Geology degrees are often called geology, earth science, applied geology or geoscience. Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.

In Nigeria, a BSc in geology is commonly a four-year programme, and many courses include a period of industrial training, often under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Some polytechnics offer ND (National Diploma) and HND (Higher National Diploma) programmes in related technical fields. In the UK, a BSc usually takes three years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and four in Scotland; integrated master’s courses such as MGeol or MSci usually add a year. In the United States a bachelor’s degree usually takes four years. Many courses end with a field camp or mapping project, and a master’s degree adds advanced courses and a research thesis.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds the language of the subject. You study Earth structure and plate tectonics, minerals and crystallography, igneous rocks and magmatism, weathering and sedimentary rocks, metamorphism and metamorphic rocks, geological time and stratigraphic principles, the basics of strike, dip, folds and faults, geological maps and field methods, and surface processes and geomorphology.

The core stage goes deeper into the same themes and adds applied subjects. It includes optical mineralogy and petrography; igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic petrology; structural geology and tectonics; stratigraphy and basin analysis; palaeontology and biostratigraphy; sedimentology and depositional systems; geochemistry and isotope geology; applied geophysics; economic geology and mineral deposits; petroleum geology; hydrogeology and groundwater; engineering geology and geohazards; environmental geology and mining; geological field mapping and exploration; and professional practice and geoscience ethics.

At master’s level, students study advanced tectonics and geodynamics, advanced basin analysis and petroleum systems, geological modelling and geostatistics, and research methods and thesis design. The order can vary, but the logic is usually from materials and processes to Earth history, then to resources, hazards and professional work.

sections.heading: How to study geology
sections.text:
Study geology by observing and recording before you interpret. In the laboratory, use a hand lens, streak plate, acid test and microscope systematically. For a rock, record colour, grain size, sorting, rounding, layering, fossils and cement before you give it a name. For a mineral, record lustre, hardness, cleavage, streak and crystal form rather than relying on colour alone.

In the field, keep a bound notebook. Record location, date, weather, rock type, orientation and sketches. Learn to read a geological map with its scale, north arrow and symbols, and practise drawing cross-sections. Link every process to its product: weathering to sediment, burial to diagenesis, heat and pressure to metamorphism. Use spaced practice for names and definitions, and work through calculations such as porosity, density and gradients until you can do them without notes. Fieldwork has hazards, so follow safety rules and never work alone in remote areas.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include memorising rock and mineral names without understanding how they form. Colour alone is a poor guide to mineral identity. Students also confuse weathering with erosion, and confuse a rock’s grains with its cement.

In map work, common errors are ignoring the scale, north arrow, strike and dip, and contour patterns. In field notes, keep observation separate from interpretation, and record uncertainty. Do not treat a simple rock cycle diagram as the whole truth. Finally, poor notes and unsafe fieldwork cost marks and can be dangerous.

keyPoints: Geology studies Earth materials, processes, history and resources, and it depends on careful field and laboratory observation.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Introductory courses build the language; core courses add petrology, tectonics, stratigraphy, geophysics and applied geology.
At master’s level, study goes deeper into tectonics, basins, modelling and research.
Record observations before interpreting, and link every process to its product.
Avoid memorising names without processes, and keep field notes clear and safe.

en.title: Earth’s interior, the rock cycle and plate tectonics
en.short: Earth’s layers and evidence, the rock cycle, and plate boundaries and their features.

sections.heading: Inside the Earth
sections.text:
Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core and inner core. The crust is about 5 to 10 km thick under oceans and up to about 70 km under some mountains. The mantle reaches about 2,900 km depth. Below it, the outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid. The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell (crust plus upper mantle); it lies on the hotter, weaker asthenosphere.

Evidence comes mainly from seismic waves. P-waves pass through solids and liquids; S-waves cannot pass through liquids. S-waves are blocked beyond about 103° from an earthquake, showing a liquid outer core. Wave speeds also change abruptly at layer boundaries, showing changes in material. Meteorites and Earth’s average density support a dense metal core.

sections.heading: The rock cycle
sections.text: The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks through processes driven by Earth’s internal heat, the sun’s energy and gravity. Weathering breaks rock into sediment; erosion and transport move it; deposition, burial, compaction and cementation form sedimentary rock. Heat and pressure change any rock into metamorphic rock. Melting produces magma, which cools to igneous rock. The cycle is not a fixed loop: rocks can skip stages, and plate tectonics recycles crust. For example, limestone can be buried, metamorphosed to marble, melted, and later crystallise as igneous rock.

sections.heading: Plate tectonics
sections.text:
Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912. He cited the fit of South America and Africa, matching fossils such as Glossopteris, rock sequences and glacial deposits. Later evidence included seafloor spreading, shown by magnetic stripes on the ocean floor and young oceanic crust near ridges, plus earthquakes at plate edges.

Plates move over the asthenosphere. At divergent boundaries they separate, forming mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys; the East African Rift is a modern example. At convergent boundaries plates move together; where a dense oceanic plate is involved, it sinks beneath the other plate (subduction). Ocean-ocean convergence gives a trench and island arc; ocean-continent gives a trench and volcanic mountain belt; continent-continent gives fold mountains. At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, producing strike-slip faults and earthquakes but little volcanism.

keyPoints: Earth’s main layers are the crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core; seismic waves reveal them.
S-waves cannot pass through liquids, which shows the outer core is liquid.
The rock cycle links igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks through weathering, burial, heat, pressure and melting.
Continental drift evidence includes matching coastlines, fossils, rocks and glacial deposits.
Seafloor magnetic stripes and ocean-floor ages support plate tectonics.
Divergent boundaries form ridges and rifts; convergent boundaries form trenches, arcs and fold mountains; transform boundaries form strike-slip faults.

en.title: Minerals and crystallography
en.short: Mineral definition, crystal systems, symmetry, silicate structures, hand-specimen properties and rock-forming groups.

sections.heading: Minerals defined
sections.text: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition, or a limited range, and an ordered internal atomic arrangement. It forms by geological processes. Ice and some biogenic crystals fit most definitions, but the boundaries vary, so check your course. The common rock-forming groups are mostly silicates, plus carbonates such as calcite, oxides such as hematite, sulphides such as pyrite, sulphates such as gypsum and halides such as halite.

sections.heading: Crystals and symmetry
sections.text: Crystals have a repeating three-dimensional lattice. The unit cell is the smallest box that repeats. Symmetry elements include rotation axes, mirror planes and a centre of symmetry. The seven crystal systems are cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and trigonal. They are defined by symmetry and by unit-cell lengths and angles. For example, cubic crystals have three equal axes at right angles and high symmetry.

sections.heading: Silicate structures
sections.text: Silicates are built from the SiO4 tetrahedron, four oxygen ions around one silicon ion. Tetrahedra may be isolated, as in olivine and garnet; linked in single chains, as in pyroxene; in double chains, as in amphibole; in sheets, as in mica and clay; or in frameworks, as in quartz and feldspar. Aluminium can replace silicon, and other ions fill charge-balancing sites. Framework silicates, especially feldspars and quartz, dominate the crust.

sections.heading: Hand-specimen properties
sections.text: Hardness is resistance to scratching. The Mohs scale runs from talc 1 to diamond 10, but it is not linear. Cleavage is breakage along weak planes fixed by structure; fracture is irregular breakage. Lustre describes reflected light, metallic or non-metallic. Streak is the colour of powder. Specific gravity is density relative to water. Amina finds a pale pink specimen that scratches glass, has two cleavages near 90 degrees and a white streak. These point to feldspar, but confirm with optical or chemical tests.

keyPoints: A mineral is naturally occurring, inorganic, solid, with a definite composition and ordered atomic structure.
The seven crystal systems are cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal and trigonal.
Silicate structures range from isolated SiO4 tetrahedra to chains, sheets and frameworks.
Mohs hardness is a scratch scale from talc 1 to diamond 10 and is not linear.
Cleavage, lustre, streak and specific gravity help identify hand specimens but need confirmation.
Feldspars, quartz, micas, amphiboles, pyroxenes, olivine and clays are the main rock-forming silicates.

en.title: Igneous rocks and magmatism
en.short: How magma forms and crystallises, Bowen’s series, igneous textures and rock names.

sections.heading: Magma and melting
sections.text:
Magma is molten rock, with dissolved gases and crystals. It forms in the mantle or crust by decompression melting, where pressure falls at a mid-ocean ridge; by adding volatiles such as water, which lowers the melting point above a subduction zone; or by heating.

Mantle melts are mafic, rich in magnesium and iron and low in silica. Crustal melts are more felsic, rich in silica, sodium and potassium.

sections.heading: Cooling and Bowen
sections.text:
Magma cools and crystallises: atoms arrange into mineral crystals. Slow cooling deep underground lets crystals grow large; rapid cooling at the surface leaves little time. Bowen’s reaction series shows the order.

Olivine, pyroxene, amphibole and biotite react with melt in a discontinuous series; plagioclase changes from calcium-rich to sodium-rich continuously. Quartz and potassium feldspar crystallise last, at lower temperatures. Removing early crystals changes the remaining melt, a process called fractional crystallisation.

sections.heading: Textures and naming
sections.text:
Texture records cooling history. Phaneritic means crystals are visible to the eye, from slow cooling in a plutonic rock, which forms underground. Aphanitic means crystals are too small to see, from rapid cooling in a volcanic rock, which forms at the surface. Porphyritic means large crystals sit in a finer matrix, from two cooling stages. Glassy means no crystals, as in obsidian. Vesicular means gas bubbles left holes, as in pumice.

Composition runs from felsic to mafic. Combine composition and grain size: granite is felsic and phaneritic; rhyolite is felsic and aphanitic; gabbro is mafic and phaneritic; basalt is mafic and aphanitic.

sections.heading: Landforms
sections.text:
Volcanic landforms include shield volcanoes, stratovolcanoes and cinder cones, plus lava plateaus and calderas. Plutonic landforms include batholiths, stocks, dykes and sills; dykes cut across rock layers and sills lie between them.

Case: the same basaltic magma in the East African Rift cools slowly in a large intrusion to gabbro, more quickly in a dyke to medium-grained dolerite, and quickly on eruption to basalt.

keyPoints: Magma forms by decompression, volatile addition or heating; mantle melts are mafic and crustal melts more felsic.
Bowen’s reaction series gives the crystallisation order: olivine and calcium plagioclase first, quartz and potassium feldspar last.
Slow cooling gives phaneritic textures; rapid cooling gives aphanitic or glassy textures.
Porphyritic texture records two cooling stages; vesicular texture records gas bubbles.
Igneous rocks are named by composition and grain size, for example granite and gabbro are phaneritic, rhyolite and basalt aphanitic.
Volcanic landforms include shield and stratovolcanoes; plutonic landforms include batholiths, dykes and sills.

en.title: Weathering, sediments and sedimentary rocks
en.short: Weathering, transport and deposition, diagenesis, the main sediment types and structures.

sections.heading: Weathering
sections.text:
Weathering breaks rock in place, without moving it. Physical (mechanical) weathering splits rock into smaller pieces: freeze-thaw, salt crystallisation, and unloading as pressure is released. Chemical weathering alters minerals: hydrolysis turns feldspar into clay, oxidation rusts iron minerals, and carbonation dissolves limestone in acidic water. Biological weathering is the work of organisms: roots prise joints apart, burrowing animals mix sediment, and lichens release organic acids.

Climate controls the balance. Warm, wet regions favour chemical weathering and produce clay and dissolved ions; cold or arid regions favour physical breakdown and leave coarse debris.

sections.heading: Erosion to lithification
sections.text:
Erosion removes the debris; transport carries it by water, wind, ice or gravity; deposition drops it when energy falls. Sediment is clastic if it is broken rock fragments, chemical if it precipitated from solution, and organic if it is built from plant or animal remains.

Diagenesis is everything that happens after deposition, at low temperature and pressure. Lithification is the part that turns loose sediment into rock: compaction squeezes water out, and cementation (calcite, quartz or iron oxide) glues the grains together.

sections.heading: Classifying the rocks
sections.text:
Sandstones are named by their grains: quartz arenite is almost all quartz; arkose is rich in feldspar; litharenite is rich in rock fragments. Mudrocks (shale, mudstone) are dominated by silt and clay, and shale splits along bedding.

Limestones are mostly calcium carbonate. Folk’s scheme uses grain types and matrix; Dunham’s uses texture, from mudstone through wackestone, packstone and grainstone to boundstone. Evaporites form when saline water dries up: gypsum, anhydrite, halite and potash salts.

sections.heading: Sedimentary structures
sections.text: Structures record how the sediment was laid down. Cross-bedding is inclined layering left by migrating ripples or dunes; graded bedding is an upward decrease in grain size from a waning current; ripples are small waves on a bed surface; mud cracks show a surface that dried out. They indicate current direction and which way up the bed is.

keyPoints: Physical weathering breaks rock without changing its minerals; chemical weathering alters them; climate controls the balance.
Clastic sediment is broken rock, chemical sediment precipitates from solution, organic sediment comes from living things.
Lithification is compaction plus cementation, and it is part of diagenesis.
Sandstone names depend on grain composition; limestone names on texture (Dunham) or grains and matrix (Folk).
Evaporites such as gypsum, anhydrite and halite form by evaporation of saline water.
Cross-bedding, graded bedding, ripples and mud cracks record current strength, direction and way-up.

en.title: Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks
en.short: Heat, pressure and fluids; contact and regional settings; textures, index minerals and rock names.

sections.heading: Agents of metamorphism
sections.text: Metamorphism is the change of a rock in the solid state, in response to heat, pressure or fluids. The original rock is the protolith. Heat, from nearby magma or from depth, drives recrystallisation and the growth of new minerals. Pressure comes in two forms: confining pressure, equal in all directions, which packs minerals more densely, and directed stress, which aligns them. Fluids, mainly water and carbon dioxide in pore spaces, carry ions and speed up reactions. Metamorphism broadly ends where melting begins; melt marks the passage into igneous processes.

sections.heading: Contact and regional settings
sections.text:
Contact (thermal) metamorphism happens around an igneous intrusion. Heat is the main agent, pressure is low, and the altered zone, called the aureole, is usually narrow. Its rock is fine-grained and non-foliated, typically hornfels.

Regional metamorphism affects whole belts during mountain building. Heat and directed pressure act together over large areas, producing foliation, and it is here that the classic sequence of grades is seen.

sections.heading: Textures and grade
sections.text:
Foliation is a layering or alignment of platy minerals such as mica and chlorite. Increasing grade gives slaty cleavage, then the coarser sheen of phyllite, then schistosity, then banding in gneiss. Non-foliated rocks are granular or hornfelsic.

Index minerals appear at particular conditions in a given bulk composition. In mud-rich (pelitic) rocks the classic sequence is chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite; each marks a higher grade, and the line where one first appears is an isograd. Grade measures intensity, not time.

sections.heading: Naming the rocks
sections.text:
Slate is fine-grained, splits along cleavage, and comes from shale. Phyllite is coarser with a silky sheen. Schist is medium to coarse and rich in visible mica. Gneiss has light and dark bands. Marble is recrystallised limestone or dolomite; hornfels is the contact rock.

Case: a mudstone bed in a fold belt becomes slate, then phyllite, then garnet schist as grade rises; the same mudstone next to a granite becomes hornfels.

keyPoints: Metamorphism is solid-state change caused by heat, pressure and fluids acting on a protolith.
Contact metamorphism is heat-dominated and gives non-foliated hornfels in a narrow aureole.
Regional metamorphism combines heat with directed stress and produces foliation over wide belts.
Foliation increases from slaty cleavage to phyllite sheen to schistosity to gneiss banding.
In pelitic rocks the index minerals run chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite, sillimanite.
Slate, schist, gneiss, marble and hornfels are named from texture and mineral content.

en.title: Geological time and stratigraphic principles
en.short: Relative dating principles, unconformities, the geological time scale and radiometric dating.

sections.heading: Relative dating
sections.text: Relative dating puts rocks and events in order without giving ages in years. Superposition: in an undisturbed sequence the oldest layer is at the bottom. Original horizontality: sediments are laid down nearly flat, so tilted layers were deformed later. Cross-cutting relationships: a fault or intrusion is younger than the rocks it cuts. Inclusions: fragments of older rock trapped in a younger host are older than that host. Faunal succession: fossils change in a consistent order, so widespread, short-lived index fossils correlate layers.

sections.heading: Unconformities
sections.text: An unconformity is a gap in the record where erosion or non-deposition removed time. An angular unconformity has tilted older layers cut by erosion and overlain by flat younger layers. A disconformity has parallel beds above and below the erosion surface. A nonconformity puts sedimentary rock on older igneous or metamorphic rock.

sections.heading: The time scale
sections.text: The geological time scale divides Earth history into eons, eras, periods and epochs, from largest to smallest. The Phanerozoic eon, the part with abundant fossils, is divided into the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic eras. Relative dating gives the order; absolute dating gives ages in years, usually with an uncertainty. The two are combined: fossils and stratigraphy give the order, and radiometric dates put numbers on it.

sections.heading: Radiometric dating
sections.text:
Radiometric dating uses radioactive decay. A parent isotope decays to a daughter product at a rate set by its half-life, the time for half the parent to decay. If the mineral stays closed, so no parent or daughter is added or lost, the parent-to-daughter ratio gives the age. The decay equation is N = N0 × (1/2)^(t/T), where N is the parent left, N0 the original amount, T the half-life and t the age.

Example: a mineral has a parent isotope with a half-life of 100 million years. If 25% of the parent remains, N/N0 = 0.25 = (1/2)², so two half-lives have passed. Age = 2 × 100 = 200 million years.

keyPoints: Superposition: in an undisturbed sequence, the oldest layer is at the bottom.
A cross-cutting fault or intrusion is younger than the rocks it cuts, and an inclusion is older than its host rock.
Unconformities are gaps in the record: angular, disconformity and nonconformity.
The geological time scale runs from eon to era to period to epoch.
Radiometric age: N = N0 × (1/2)^(t/T); 25% parent left means two half-lives.
Relative dating gives order; absolute dating gives ages in years with uncertainty.

en.title: Structural geology: strike, dip, folds and faults
en.short: Strike and dip, map symbols, folds, faults and joints: how to measure and recognise them.

sections.heading: Strike and dip
sections.text:
Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on a bedding plane. Dip is the angle between the plane and horizontal, measured perpendicular to strike in the steepest direction. A compass-clinometer gives both; note the dip direction.

The map symbol is a line along strike with a short tick pointing downdip, labelled with the dip, for example 30°.

Apparent dip is seen in a section not perpendicular to strike: tan(apparent dip) = tan(true dip) × sin(angle between section line and strike). Example: true dip 30°, section at 40° to strike: 0.5774 × 0.6428 = 0.3712, so apparent dip = 20.4°.

sections.heading: Folds
sections.text:
An anticline arches upward with oldest strata in its core; a syncline arches downward with youngest strata in its core. A monocline is a single step-like bend in otherwise gently dipping strata. Parts are the two limbs, the hinge line of greatest curvature, and the axial plane through the hinges.

Recognition: matching strata across the fold, younging direction (which way up the beds are) from sedimentary structures, and map patterns. Beds often form V shapes in valleys; the V points according to dip and valley slope.

sections.heading: Faults
sections.text:
A fault is a fracture along which rock has moved. The hanging wall lies above the fault plane, the footwall below. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down, usually under extension. In a reverse fault it moves up, under compression; a low-angle reverse fault is a thrust. In a strike-slip fault the walls move horizontally past each other, dextral (right-lateral) or sinistral (left-lateral) as seen from one side.

Recognition: offset beds or markers, slickensides (polished, grooved fault surfaces), drag folds, fault breccia or gouge (fine crushed rock), and scarps. Strata in boreholes may be repeated or omitted.

sections.heading: Joints and fractures
sections.text: Joints are fractures with no visible displacement. A set is a group with similar orientation; several sets form a joint system. Examples include columnar joints in lava and sheeting in granite. Joints control permeability, rock strength and slope stability. A fracture with displacement is a fault.

keyPoints: Strike is the compass direction of a horizontal line on a plane; dip is the steepest angle from horizontal, perpendicular to strike.
On maps, strike and dip are shown by a strike line with a downdip tick and the dip angle.
tan(apparent dip) = tan(true dip) × sin(angle between section line and strike); apparent dip is never greater than true dip.
Anticlines have oldest rocks in the core, synclines youngest; monoclines are single step-like bends.
Normal faults have the hanging wall down, reverse faults have it up, and strike-slip faults move horizontally.
Joints are fractures with no visible displacement; a fracture with displacement is a fault.

en.title: Geological maps, cross-sections and field methods
en.short: Map symbols, cross-sections, outcrop patterns, compass-clinometer, GPS, notebook, sampling and safety.

sections.heading: Reading maps
sections.text: A geological map shows rock units, boundaries and structures on a topographic base. Check the scale, north arrow, grid and legend first. The scale 1:50,000 means 1 cm on the map equals 50,000 cm, or 500 m, on the ground; so 2 cm is 1 km. Strike and dip describe the orientation of a plane: strike is the direction of a horizontal line on the plane, and dip is the angle it slopes down from horizontal, measured at right angles to the strike. On the map symbol, the long line is strike, the short tick points downdip, and the number is the dip angle. Outcrop patterns depend on topography and dip. Horizontal beds tend to follow contours; dipping beds cut across them, forming V shapes in valleys.

sections.heading: Cross-sections
sections.text: A cross-section is a vertical slice through the map. Draw a section line across the map, transfer the topography to a profile, then mark where rock boundaries cross the line. Choose a vertical scale and calculate the vertical exaggeration: VE = horizontal scale ÷ vertical scale. For example, horizontal 1:50,000 and vertical 1:10,000 give VE = 50,000 ÷ 10,000 = 5. Plot boundaries using their dip angles, adjusting the angles if the section is vertically exaggerated, and extend them downward only as far as the evidence allows. Keep the horizontal and vertical scales labelled.

sections.heading: Field tools
sections.text: A compass-clinometer measures the orientation of a plane. Place its long edge on the bedding plane, level it, and read strike; then turn 90° and use the clinometer to read dip. A GPS gives your position; record the coordinates and the datum, usually WGS84, and check it matches your map. The field notebook is your main record: date, time, weather, location, rock description, sketches, sample numbers and measurements. Write in pencil or waterproof ink, and never rely on memory.

sections.heading: Sampling and safety
sections.text: Take samples that represent the rock unit, not just the unusual piece. Label each with a unique number, location, orientation if needed, and field description. For safety, do a risk assessment before you go: tell someone your route and return time, work in a buddy system, carry water, food, first aid, sun protection and a charged phone. Check the weather, respect local permissions and avoid steep or unstable ground.

keyPoints: Map scale converts map distance to ground distance: at 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map is 500 m on the ground.
In a strike and dip symbol, the long line is strike, the short tick points downdip, and the number is the dip angle.
Vertical exaggeration = horizontal scale ÷ vertical scale; 1:50,000 horizontal and 1:10,000 vertical give 5.
A compass-clinometer measures strike and dip; a GPS records position and map datum.
The field notebook should record date, location, rock description, measurements and sample numbers.
Take representative samples, label them clearly, and follow a risk assessment and buddy system in the field.

en.title: Earth surface processes and geomorphology
en.short: How weathering, erosion and rivers, coasts, wind, ice, karst and slopes shape landforms.

sections.heading: Weathering and erosion
sections.text:
Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion removes the debris and transports it. Physical weathering includes freeze-thaw and salt growth; chemical weathering includes dissolution and hydrolysis. Rock type and climate decide which process dominates: freeze-thaw is strong in cold mountains, hydrolysis in warm wet regions. Both prepare material for erosion, so landscapes reflect the balance between rock resistance, climate and time.

Erosion by water, wind, ice and waves lowers the land and moves sediment to basins. Deposition builds new landforms where transport energy falls. Together, weathering and erosion wear down mountains and fill lowlands.

sections.heading: Rivers, coasts and wind
sections.text:
Fluvial processes erode, transport and deposit sediment. Rivers cut valleys, meander across floodplains and build deltas and alluvial fans where gradient and flow slacken.

Coasts are shaped by waves, tides and longshore drift, the movement of sediment along the shore. This forms cliffs, beaches, spits and stacks. Wind, or aeolian action, erodes by deflation and abrasion; its deposits form dunes and, far from source, loess.

sections.heading: Ice, karst and slopes
sections.text: Glaciers erode and deposit. They carve U-shaped valleys and leave moraines, drumlins, eskers and erratics. Karst develops where limestone dissolves: sinkholes, caves and underground drainage form. On slopes, gravity moves material by creep, falls, slides and flows; water reduces strength and can trigger failure. A landslide is any rapid downslope movement of rock and soil; a fall is a free drop from a cliff.

sections.heading: Drainage and the Quaternary
sections.text:
Drainage patterns record structure and history: dendritic on uniform rock, trellis on folded strata, radial around a peak, rectangular on jointed rock. Drainage density is channel length divided by area; it rises where rock is impermeable and relief is steep. Example: 50 km of channels in 20 km² gives 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 km/km².

The Quaternary is the most recent period, divided into the Pleistocene and Holocene. Pleistocene glaciations left moraines, river terraces, raised beaches and loess in many regions. These landforms help date recent landscape change.

keyPoints: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion removes and transports the debris.
Rivers, coasts, wind, ice and groundwater each erode, transport and deposit sediment, producing characteristic landforms.
Drainage patterns reflect rock structure and history; drainage density = channel length ÷ area.
Slope processes include creep, falls, slides and flows, often triggered when water reduces strength.
Glaciers carve U-shaped valleys and leave moraines, drumlins, eskers and erratics; karst forms by limestone dissolution.
The Quaternary (Pleistocene and Holocene) left moraines, river terraces, raised beaches and loess that help date recent landscape change.

en.title: Optical mineralogy and petrography
en.short: The polarising microscope, optical mineral properties and describing rock textures in thin section.

sections.heading: Polarising microscope
sections.text:
A polarising microscope passes plane-polarised light through a thin section, a rock slice about 30 micrometres thick. The polariser is below the stage; the analyser is above. With analyser out you see relief, cleavage and colour. With analyser in (crossed polars) you see interference colours and extinction. The stage rotates to measure angles.

Isotropic minerals, such as cubic minerals, have one refractive index and stay dark under crossed polars at all rotations. Anisotropic minerals have two or three refractive indices; they brighten and go extinct as the stage turns. Relief is the contrast between a grain and the mounting medium, usually Canada balsam with refractive index about 1.54.

sections.heading: Optical properties
sections.text:
Cleavage shows as straight traces; the angle between sets helps separate pyroxene (near 90°) from amphibole (near 60°/120°). Twinning appears as stripes or patches: plagioclase has albite twinning, microcline has gridiron twinning. Extinction is the dark position under crossed polars; anisotropic minerals extinguish every 90° of rotation. The extinction angle, from cleavage, is diagnostic.

Interference colour depends on retardation Δ = d × (n₂ − n₁), where d is thickness and n₂ − n₁ is birefringence. For quartz, birefringence ≈ 0.009 and d = 30 µm = 30,000 nm, so Δ = 0.009 × 30,000 = 270 nm, a first-order white/yellow. Higher orders need an accessory plate or the Michel-Lévy chart.

sections.heading: Identifying minerals
sections.text: Quartz: low relief, no cleavage, low birefringence, undulose extinction. Plagioclase: twinning, low relief. Biotite: brown pleochroism, high birefringence, one cleavage. Amphibole: green pleochroism, 60°/120° cleavage. Olivine: high relief, fractures. Calcite: extreme birefringence, rhombohedral cleavage, twinning. Always confirm with several properties, not one.

sections.heading: Describing textures
sections.text: Texture means grain size, shape and arrangement. Igneous textures include equigranular, porphyritic, ophitic and vesicular. Sedimentary textures record grain size, sorting, roundness, matrix and cement. Metamorphic textures include foliation, schistosity, granoblastic (interlocking grains) and porphyroblastic (large crystals in finer matrix). In a granite thin section, quartz shows undulose extinction, plagioclase shows albite twinning and biotite shows brown pleochroism.

keyPoints: Under crossed polars, isotropic minerals stay dark at all rotations; anisotropic minerals show interference colours and go extinct every 90°.
Relief is set by the refractive index difference between the mineral and the mounting medium, usually Canada balsam (n ≈ 1.54).
Retardation Δ = thickness × birefringence; a standard 30 µm section of quartz (birefringence ≈ 0.009) gives Δ ≈ 270 nm.
Cleavage angles and extinction angles help distinguish pyroxene from amphibole and other mafic minerals.
Twinning patterns, such as albite twinning in plagioclase, are diagnostic in thin section.
Texture describes grain size, shape and arrangement; record it for igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

en.title: Igneous petrology
en.short: Magma types and settings, differentiation, phase diagrams, IUGS and TAS classification, textures and rock series.

sections.heading: Magma types and settings
sections.text:
Magmas are grouped by silica and alkali content. Basaltic magma is low in silica and hot; andesitic magma is intermediate; dacitic and rhyolitic magmas are silica-rich (felsic) and cooler. The names refer mainly to volcanic rocks.

Tectonic setting helps explain them. Mid-ocean ridges produce tholeiitic basalt (MORB). Hotspots produce ocean-island basalt. Subduction zones produce hydrous, calc-alkaline magmas, from basalt through andesite to dacite and rhyolite. Continental collision and thickened crust produce granitic melts. These links are general, not fixed rules.

sections.heading: Differentiation processes
sections.text: Fractional crystallisation removes early-formed crystals from melt, so the remaining liquid becomes richer in silica and incompatible elements, which stay in the melt rather than enter early crystals. Assimilation incorporates wall rock into magma and shifts its composition, commonly raising silica or volatiles. Magma mixing blends two magmas; disequilibrium textures such as resorbed crystals or oscillatory zoning may record it. All three can operate together.

sections.heading: Phase diagrams and classification
sections.text:
Binary phase diagrams plot temperature against composition. A eutectic is the lowest melting point on a simple two-component system; the lever rule gives phase proportions at a given temperature. Example: bulk 40% B, melt 20% B, solid 80% B. Melt fraction = (80 − 40) ÷ (80 − 20) = 0.67, so 67% melt and 33% solid.

Ternary diagrams add a third component and show cotectic lines where two crystals coexist with melt. IUGS classification uses modal minerals, especially quartz, alkali feldspar and plagioclase for plutonic rocks. The TAS diagram plots total alkalis against silica for volcanic rocks. Both schemes need fresh, representative analyses.

sections.heading: Textures and rock series
sections.text: Volcanic textures record rapid cooling near the surface: glass, a fine groundmass and vesicles. Phenocrysts are large crystals that grew slowly at depth before eruption. Plutonic textures record slow cooling: coarse, equigranular crystals and cumulate layers of settled crystals. The main series are tholeiitic, calc-alkaline and alkaline. They differ in iron enrichment and alkali content.

keyPoints: Basaltic, andesitic, dacitic and rhyolitic magmas broadly track silica content and tectonic setting.
Fractional crystallisation, assimilation and magma mixing can change melt composition.
Lever rule: melt fraction = (C_solid − C_bulk) ÷ (C_solid − C_melt).
Binary diagrams show eutectics; ternary diagrams show cotectics.
IUGS uses modal minerals; TAS uses total alkalis against silica for volcanic rocks.
Volcanic textures are fine-grained or glassy; plutonic textures are coarse-grained.

en.title: Sedimentary petrology and diagenesis
en.short: Provenance, sandstone and mudrock names, carbonate textures, and diagenetic controls on porosity.

sections.heading: Provenance and maturity
sections.text: Provenance is the source area and history of sediment. It is read from framework grains, heavy minerals (dense grains such as zircon) and geochemistry. Compositional maturity means the sediment is rich in stable quartz and poor in feldspar and rock fragments (lithics). Textural maturity means well sorted, rounded grains with little fine matrix. Long transport and strong weathering usually raise both, but source rock, climate and depositional setting also matter.

sections.heading: Sand and mud names
sections.text: Sandstone classification uses framework grains. A quartz arenite is quartz-rich; an arkose is feldspar-rich; a litharenite is lithic-rich. Mudrock is fine-grained rock made of silt and clay. Claystone is clay-rich, siltstone is silt-rich, mudstone is a non-fissile mudrock, and shale is a fissile mudrock, one that splits into thin layers. Names depend on composition and texture, not colour alone.

sections.heading: Carbonate textures
sections.text: Carbonate classification is based on depositional texture. Dunham’s scheme uses mud support and grain support: mudstone, wackestone, packstone, grainstone and boundstone. Folk’s scheme names the allochems, the sand-sized grains (ooids, fossils, pellets, intraclasts), and the matrix or cement (micrite, lime mud, or sparite, clear cement), giving names such as oosparite and biomicrite. These names describe the rock before later alteration.

sections.heading: Diagenesis and pores
sections.text: Diagenesis is all change after deposition and before metamorphism. Compaction squeezes grains and reduces porosity. Cementation fills pores with minerals such as calcite or quartz. Dissolution creates secondary pores. Dolomitisation replaces calcite with dolomite and may raise or lower porosity. Porosity is the fraction of void space; permeability is the ease of flow, controlled by pore connectivity. Compaction and cementation lower permeability; dissolution may improve it. Example: 100 cm³ of sandstone with 30 cm³ pores has 30% porosity. If cement fills 10 cm³, porosity becomes 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.

keyPoints: Provenance is the source and history of sediment; compositional maturity means quartz-rich and feldspar- and lithic-poor.
Sandstones are named by framework grains, such as quartz arenite, arkose and litharenite; mudrocks by grain size and fissility.
Dunham uses depositional texture and mud or grain support; Folk uses allochems plus micrite or sparite.
Compaction and cementation reduce porosity and permeability; dissolution creates secondary porosity.
Dolomitisation can increase or decrease porosity depending on the volume replaced and the crystal fabric.
Porosity = pore volume ÷ bulk volume; 30 cm³ of pores in 100 cm³ of rock is 30%, and filling 10 cm³ leaves 20%.

en.title: Metamorphic petrology: reactions, facies and fabrics
en.short: Reactions, facies series, P-T-t paths, thermobarometry, fabrics and metamorphic rock names.

sections.heading: Reactions and equilibrium
sections.text:
Metamorphic reactions happen in the solid state, commonly by recrystallisation, polymorphic change or devolatilisation. Equilibrium means the forward and reverse reactions balance, so the stable mineral assemblage records the pressure and temperature (P-T) at that moment. The driving quantity is Gibbs energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so T = ΔH ÷ ΔS.

Example: if ΔH = 80 kJ/mol and ΔS = 0.08 kJ/(mol·K), then T = 80 ÷ 0.08 = 1000 K. Real rocks often fail to reach equilibrium; zoned minerals and reaction rims record changing conditions.

sections.heading: Facies and P-T-t paths
sections.text:
A metamorphic facies is a set of mineral assemblages that recur in rocks of similar bulk composition under a similar P-T range. A facies series is the sequence of facies produced along a particular geothermal gradient, such as low-P, medium-P or high-P series. The P-T-t path adds time: it traces burial, heating, deformation and exhumation.

Thermobarometry estimates P and T from the compositions of coexisting minerals that equilibrated together. Exchange reactions, such as Fe-Mg exchange between garnet and biotite, are used as thermometers; net-transfer reactions are used as barometers. Results carry uncertainty and must be checked against textures.

sections.heading: Textures, fabrics and names
sections.text:
Foliation is a planar fabric formed by aligned platy minerals or compositional layering. Lineation is a linear fabric, such as aligned needles or stretched pebbles. A porphyroblast is a large crystal grown during metamorphism in a finer matrix; its inclusion trails can record deformation history.

The protolith is the parent rock. Names combine fabric and protolith: shale becomes slate, phyllite, schist or gneiss with increasing grade; limestone becomes marble; sandstone becomes quartzite; basalt becomes greenschist, amphibolite or eclogite. Hornfels is a contact-metamorphic rock with a granular fabric.

keyPoints: At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so T = ΔH ÷ ΔS for a reaction with known ΔH and ΔS.
A metamorphic facies is a recurring assemblage for a bulk composition and P-T range; a facies series follows a geothermal gradient.
P-T-t paths record burial, heating and exhumation through time.
Thermobarometry uses coexisting mineral compositions, but results depend on equilibrium and calibration uncertainty.
Foliation is planar, lineation is linear, and porphyroblasts are large metamorphic crystals in a finer matrix.
Rock names link protolith and fabric, for example shale to slate, schist or gneiss, and limestone to marble.

en.title: Structural geology and tectonics
en.short: Stress, strain, deformation mechanisms, folds, faults, shear zones, stereonets, balanced sections and plate boundaries.

sections.heading: Stress and strain
sections.text:
Stress is force per unit area; it is a tensor quantity. Normal stress acts perpendicular to a plane, shear stress parallel to it. Strain is change in shape or size. Elastic strain recovers; permanent strain is plastic or viscous. Finite strain is described by principal stretches and the strain ellipsoid.

Example: a bed 2.00 m long shortens to 1.80 m. e = (l − l0) ÷ l0 = (1.80 − 2.00) ÷ 2.00 = −0.10, a 10% shortening.

sections.heading: Brittle and ductile
sections.text: Brittle deformation is fracturing and frictional sliding. It dominates at low temperature, low confining pressure, fast strain and in strong rocks. Ductile deformation is distributed flow by crystal plasticity, diffusion creep or grain-boundary sliding. It dominates at higher temperature and pressure, slower strain and in weak minerals. Mechanisms include cataclasis (brittle), pressure solution, dynamic recrystallisation and dislocation creep. Many rocks show both, with a gradual transition.

sections.heading: Folds, faults, shear zones
sections.text: Folds are analysed by hinge line, axial surface and interlimb angle; vergence indicates transport direction and fold superposition shows the sequence of deformation events. Faults are classified by dip and slip: normal faults extend, reverse and thrust faults shorten, strike-slip faults slide horizontally. Fault analysis uses slip vectors, slickensides and cut-off lines. Shear zones are tabular zones of concentrated ductile strain; asymmetric porphyroclasts, S-C fabrics and rotated markers give the sense of shear.

sections.heading: Stereonets and boundaries
sections.text: A stereographic projection plots planes as great circles and lines as points on a projected sphere; it finds fold axes, fault slip and stress directions. A balanced cross-section conserves bed length or area, so it can be restored and tested. It is valid only if the section is perpendicular to structure and no material has moved in or out. At plate boundaries, divergent margins produce normal faults and rift basins, convergent margins produce thrusts, folds and shear zones, and transform margins produce strike-slip faults. Orogenic belts stack thrust sheets, fold strata and exhume deeper rocks.

keyPoints: Stress is force per unit area and is a tensor; strain is change in shape or size.
Elongation e = (l − l0) ÷ l0; negative e means shortening.
Brittle deformation dominates at low temperature, low pressure and fast strain; ductile deformation at higher temperature and slower strain.
Folds are described by hinge line, axial surface and interlimb angle; faults by dip and slip.
A balanced cross-section conserves bed length or area and must be restorable.
Stereographic projection plots planes as great circles and lines as points; plate boundaries have characteristic structures.

en.title: Stratigraphy and basin analysis
en.short: Stratigraphic units, correlation, sequence stratigraphy, subsidence and basin fill.

sections.heading: Stratigraphic frameworks
sections.text: Lithostratigraphy names rock bodies by lithology, such as formations, members and groups; boundaries may cross time. Biostratigraphy uses fossil zones and first or last appearances; zones can be diachronous. Chronostratigraphy divides rocks by age into systems, series and stages, with Global Boundary Stratotype Sections and Points (GSSPs). Magnetostratigraphy uses polarity chrons from reversals, calibrated by radiometric dates and fossils. Correlation links units between places using lithology, fossils, polarity, sequence surfaces and chemostratigraphy; no single method is enough.

sections.heading: Sequence stratigraphy
sections.text: Sequence stratigraphy interprets strata in terms of accommodation, the space available for sediment, relative sea level and sediment supply. A depositional sequence is bounded by unconformities or correlative conformities. Systems tracts are lowstand, transgressive, highstand and falling-stage; each has a characteristic stacking pattern. Models differ, including the Exxon depositional sequence and genetic stratigraphy, so use local data.

sections.heading: Subsidence and basins
sections.text: Subsidence creates accommodation. Mechanisms include crustal stretching and thinning, flexure under sediment or thrust loads, and dynamic mantle support. Basin types include rift, passive margin, foreland, forearc, backarc, intracratonic and pull-apart. A simple water-loaded stretching calculation is S = h(1 − 1/β)(ρm − ρc)/(ρm − ρw), where h is initial crustal thickness and β is the stretching factor. With h = 30 km, β = 2, ρm = 3300, ρc = 2800 and ρw = 1000 kg/m³, S = 30 × 0.5 × 500 ÷ 2300 = 3.26 km.

sections.heading: Basin fill and setting
sections.text: Basin fill records tectonic setting through provenance, sediment composition, facies and geometry. Rift basins commonly fill with coarse clastics and lacustrine muds; passive margins with deltas and carbonates; foreland basins with wedge-shaped clastics. These are models, so compare several lines of evidence before assigning a setting.

keyPoints: Lithostratigraphy is based on lithology; chronostratigraphy is based on age.
Biostratigraphic zones use fossil ranges and may be diachronous.
Magnetostratigraphy uses reversal polarity chrons calibrated by dates.
Sequence stratigraphy links accommodation, relative sea level and sediment supply; systems tracts are lowstand, transgressive, highstand and falling-stage.
Water-loaded subsidence from stretching is S = h(1 − 1/β)(ρm − ρc)/(ρm − ρw).
Basin type and fill reflect tectonic setting, but interpretations need multiple evidence lines.

en.title: Palaeontology and biostratigraphy
en.short: How fossils form, the main fossil groups, evolution, biostratigraphic zones and palaeoenvironmental interpretation.

sections.heading: Fossil groups
sections.text: Body fossils are remains of organisms; trace fossils record activity such as burrows and footprints. Major groups include invertebrates with shells or skeletons (brachiopods, molluscs such as ammonites, trilobites, corals, echinoderms), vertebrates, plants, and microfossils such as foraminifera, conodonts and pollen. Their morphology (form and structure), for example shell shape, ribs, chambers, sutures, teeth and leaf form, reflects function and environment. Soft parts are rarely preserved.

sections.heading: Fossilisation and taphonomy
sections.text: Fossilisation needs rapid burial and hard parts. Common modes are permineralisation (minerals fill pore spaces), replacement (minerals replace the skeleton), moulds and casts (the shell dissolves and may be filled), carbonisation, and preservation in amber or tar. Taphonomy studies the path from death to discovery: transport, breakage, decay, scavenging and later change (diagenesis). These processes bias assemblages, so a fossil bed is not a complete census of the living community.

sections.heading: Evolution and biostratigraphy
sections.text: The fossil record shows descent with modification, extinction and turnover, but it is incomplete. Biostratigraphy uses fossils to divide and correlate rock. A biozone is a body of rock defined by its fossil content. A good index fossil is abundant, widespread, short-lived and easy to identify. Example: if a sample has 40 specimens and 10 belong to species A, A is 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25% of the assemblage. That abundance may help define an assemblage zone, but the zone still needs a stated boundary and range.

sections.heading: Palaeoenvironment
sections.text: Palaeoecology reconstructs past life and environments from fossils and their context. Functional morphology suggests habit, for example a thick shell may resist wave action. Assemblage composition indicates salinity, depth, temperature, substrate and oxygen. Taphonomy must be assessed first, because transport can mix deep and shallow species. The result is an interpretation, not a direct measurement.

keyPoints: Body fossils preserve hard parts; trace fossils record activity.
Fossilisation usually requires rapid burial and hard parts; taphonomy explains bias.
Major groups include shelly invertebrates, vertebrates, plants and microfossils.
Biostratigraphy correlates rocks using fossil ranges and assemblages.
A good index fossil is abundant, widespread, short-lived and easy to identify.
Palaeoecology uses morphology, assemblage data and taphonomy to infer environment.

en.title: Sedimentology and depositional systems
en.short: Facies, clastic and carbonate systems, sedimentary structures, and facies models for correlation.

sections.heading: Facies and associations
sections.text:
A facies is a body of sediment or rock defined by its lithology, grain size, sedimentary structures and fossils, reflecting a particular depositional environment. A facies association is a group of facies that occur together and are genetically linked, such as channel and floodplain deposits.

Walther’s law states that in a conformable succession, vertical facies changes record the lateral migration of environments. This is why a fining-upward fluvial channel can pass up into floodplain muds.

sections.heading: Clastic systems
sections.text:
Fluvial systems have channels, point bars and floodplains; point bars fine upward and show trough cross-bedding. Deltaic systems form where a river enters standing water, with distributary channels, mouth bars and prodelta muds, commonly coarsening upward. Coastal systems include beaches, barriers and tidal flats, with wave ripples, herringbone cross-bedding from reversing tidal currents, and burrows. Shallow-marine shelves show storm beds and bioturbation.

Deep-marine systems are dominated by turbidity currents; their deposits are graded beds and the Bouma sequence, a standard upward order from graded sand to overlying mud.

sections.heading: Carbonate and evaporite systems
sections.text:
Carbonate systems form mainly in warm, clear, shallow seas where light and low siliciclastic input allow reefs, ooids (coated carbonate grains) and lime mud. Evaporite systems form in arid basins with restricted inflow, depositing gypsum, anhydrite and halite as water evaporates.

Both are sensitive to salinity and water depth, so their facies are useful environmental indicators.

sections.heading: Models and correlation
sections.text:
Sedimentary structures are read as process indicators: cross-bedding records migrating bedforms, graded bedding records waning flows, mud cracks record exposure, and bioturbation records slow deposition. A facies model is an idealised summary of a depositional system.

It is used to predict facies away from control points and to correlate outcrops or wells. A hypothetical coastal cliff in Ghana might show beach sandstone passing up into tidal-flat muds; the model predicts the lateral equivalents. Models guide interpretation but must be tested against local data.

keyPoints: A facies is defined by lithology, sedimentary structures and fossils and reflects a depositional environment.
Facies associations group genetically related facies and are the basis of facies models.
Walther’s law links vertical facies successions to lateral migration of environments in conformable successions.
Fluvial and deltaic systems commonly show fining-upward and coarsening-upward trends respectively.
Sedimentary structures such as cross-bedding, graded bedding, mud cracks and bioturbation indicate processes and conditions.
Facies models are predictive tools for correlation, not rigid templates.

en.title: Geochemistry and isotope geology
en.short: Element behaviour, stable and radiogenic isotopes, dating methods and their geological uses.

sections.heading: Element behaviour
sections.text: Major elements form the main rock-forming minerals and are reported as oxides. Trace elements occur at parts per million or less; their behaviour is summarised by the partition coefficient D, the concentration in a mineral divided by that in melt. Incompatible elements prefer melt, compatible elements prefer crystals. Rare earth elements (REE) form a smooth series; plotting chondrite-normalised abundances shows light-to-heavy slopes and Eu anomalies, which record feldspar removal or accumulation.

sections.heading: Stable isotopes
sections.text: Stable isotope fractionation separates isotopes by mass during physical and chemical processes. Results use delta notation: δ = (R_sample ÷ R_standard − 1) × 1000, in per mil. Lighter isotopes usually react faster, so temperature, evaporation and biological uptake change δ. Oxygen and hydrogen in water and ice track temperature and rainfall; carbon in carbonates and organic matter tracks carbon cycling; sulphur in sulphides and sulphates tracks redox and microbial processes.

sections.heading: Radiogenic clocks
sections.text: Radiogenic isotopes form by radioactive decay. The age equation is D* = N(e^λt − 1), where D* is daughter from decay, N is parent atoms now and λ is the decay constant. Rb-Sr and Sm-Nd use isochrons; U-Pb gives concordia ages and is robust; K-Ar and Ar-Ar date cooling below a closure temperature. Example: for Rb-Sr with λ = 1.42 × 10^-11 yr^-1 and isochron slope m = e^λt − 1 = 0.05, t = ln(1.05) ÷ (1.42 × 10^-11) = 3.44 × 10^9 years.

sections.heading: Methods and uses
sections.text: Samples are prepared in clean laboratories and measured by thermal ionisation mass spectrometry (TIMS), multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (MC-ICP-MS) or gas-source mass spectrometry. Applications include petrogenesis: isotopes distinguish mantle sources and crustal contamination. Provenance: detrital zircon U-Pb ages and Sm-Nd model ages link sediments to source terrains. Palaeoclimate: oxygen and carbon isotope records in ice, corals and foraminifera reconstruct temperature, ice volume and carbon cycling.

keyPoints: Partition coefficient D = C_mineral ÷ C_melt; incompatible elements have low D and concentrate in melts.
Chondrite-normalised REE patterns show light-to-heavy slopes and Eu anomalies.
Stable isotope data use δ = (R_sample ÷ R_standard − 1) × 1000 per mil.
Radiogenic age equation: D* = N(e^λt − 1); isochron slope m = e^λt − 1.
Rb-Sr, Sm-Nd, U-Pb and K-Ar have different closure temperatures and mineral uses.
TIMS, MC-ICP-MS and gas-source mass spectrometry are standard analytical methods.

en.title: Applied geophysics
en.short: Covers seismic, gravity, magnetic, electrical, electromagnetic and borehole methods for subsurface investigation.

sections.heading: Seismic methods
sections.text: Seismic methods use elastic waves made by a hammer, explosive or vibrator. Refraction records the first arrival at each receiver. Where a deeper layer is faster, waves bend along the interface and return; travel-time graphs give layer velocities and depths. Reflection records later echoes from boundaries and is processed into images of structure. Reflection strength depends on acoustic impedance, the product of density and wave speed.

sections.heading: Potential and electrical methods
sections.text: Gravity surveys measure small changes in gravitational acceleration caused by density contrasts. Magnetic surveys measure anomalies in the Earth’s field caused by magnetic minerals, especially magnetite. Gravity data need corrections for latitude, elevation and terrain; magnetic data need diurnal and main-field corrections. Electrical resistivity injects current through electrodes and measures voltage; apparent resistivity depends on the array and subsurface. Electromagnetic methods induce currents and measure the secondary field, giving conductivity. Ground-penetrating radar is an electromagnetic method for shallow targets.

sections.heading: Borehole logging
sections.text: Borehole logging lowers instruments into a hole to measure properties continuously with depth. Natural gamma log indicates clay content; resistivity logs distinguish fluid and rock; density and neutron logs estimate porosity; sonic logs give wave speed; caliper logs show hole diameter. Logs are corrected, depth-matched and interpreted with core and cuttings.

sections.heading: Interpretation and applications
sections.text:
Processing applies corrections and removes noise, then modelling or inversion converts measurements into a subsurface model. Interpretation combines geology and several methods. Mineral exploration uses magnetic and gravity anomalies and induced polarisation for sulphides. Groundwater work uses resistivity and electromagnetics to find aquifers and salinity. Engineering uses refraction for depth to bedrock and rippability, and radar for utilities.

Worked example: a two-layer refraction survey has v1 = 1,000 m/s, v2 = 3,000 m/s and intercept time ti = 0.020 s. Depth z = ti v1 v2 ÷ (2√(v2² − v1²)) = 0.020 × 1,000 × 3,000 ÷ (2 × √(3,000² − 1,000²)) = 60,000 ÷ 5,656.85 = 10.6 m.

keyPoints: Seismic refraction uses first-arrival travel times to find layer velocities and depths; reflection images boundaries.
Gravity and magnetic surveys map density and magnetic-susceptibility contrasts after corrections.
Electrical resistivity and electromagnetic methods map conductivity, useful for groundwater and salinity.
Borehole logs give continuous depth records of lithology, porosity and fluid properties.
Two-layer refraction depth: z = ti v1 v2 ÷ (2√(v2² − v1²)).
Always correct, model and integrate geophysical results with geological and borehole data.

en.title: Economic geology and mineral deposits
en.short: Ore-forming processes, deposit types, industrial minerals, exploration and resource classification.

sections.heading: Ore-forming processes
sections.text: An ore is rock containing valuable minerals that can be mined at a profit; gangue is the waste mineral matter. Grade is the concentration of the valuable element or mineral, and cut-off grade is the lowest grade that pays. Magmatic processes concentrate metals in cooling magma, as in chromite layers or nickel-copper sulphide deposits. Hydrothermal processes use hot aqueous fluids to carry and deposit metals in veins, breccias and replacements. Sedimentary processes form deposits by precipitation, evaporation or sorting, such as banded iron formation, evaporites and placers. Supergene processes enrich metals by weathering and groundwater, producing laterite and secondary sulphide zones.

sections.heading: Deposit types
sections.text: Main deposit types include porphyry copper-gold-molybdenum, epithermal gold-silver, volcanogenic massive sulphide, sedimentary exhalative, Mississippi Valley-type lead-zinc, banded iron formation, laterite nickel, and placer gold or tin. Industrial minerals are rocks or minerals valued for their properties, not mainly for metal: limestone for cement, gypsum, kaolin, silica sand, phosphate and salt. Aggregates are crushed rock, sand and gravel used in construction. They are bulky and low value, so transport cost makes location critical.

sections.heading: Exploration and classification
sections.text: Exploration combines geological mapping, geochemical sampling, geophysics and drilling. Assays must pass quality control. A mineral resource is a concentration with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction; it is classified as inferred, indicated or measured according to confidence. A reserve is the economically mineable part of measured or indicated resources, classified as probable or proved. Codes differ by country, for example JORC in Australia and SAMREC in South Africa; check the current code.

sections.heading: Mining geology and grade control
sections.text: Mining geology uses close-spaced sampling, mapping and assay to separate ore from waste, control dilution (waste rock mixed into ore) and reconcile predicted with mined grades. Example: 1,000,000 t at 2.0% copper contains 1,000,000 × 0.02 = 20,000 t Cu. At 90% recovery, 18,000 t Cu is recoverable. A 1% cut-off means material below 1% Cu is treated as waste, unless blending with higher-grade ore makes it pay; cut-off grades change with metal prices and costs.

keyPoints: Ore is rock that can be mined at a profit; grade is the valuable content and cut-off grade is the lowest economic grade.
Magmatic, hydrothermal, sedimentary and supergene processes concentrate metals in different geological settings.
Main deposit types include porphyry, epithermal, VMS, SEDEX, MVT, BIF, laterite and placers.
Industrial minerals and aggregates are valued for properties and location, and transport cost is often critical.
Resources are inferred, indicated or measured; reserves are probable or proved and must be economic.
Contained metal = ore tonnage × grade; recoverable metal = contained metal × recovery.

en.title: Petroleum geology
en.short: Source rocks, kerogen, maturation, migration, reservoirs, seals, traps, basin modelling and exploration.

sections.heading: Source rocks and kerogen
sections.text:
A source rock is a fine-grained, organic-rich sediment, commonly shale or limestone, deposited where oxygen is low enough to preserve organic matter. Its quality is judged by total organic carbon (TOC) and by kerogen, the insoluble organic matter left after bitumen is removed.

Kerogen types: Type I is algal and lacustrine, very oil-prone; Type II is marine and oil- to gas-prone; Type III comes from land plants and is gas-prone; Type IV is inert. Rock-Eval pyrolysis and the hydrogen index help identify them.

sections.heading: Maturation and migration
sections.text:
Burial raises temperature. The oil window is roughly 60 to 120 °C and the gas window roughly 120 to 200 °C, but the limits shift with heating rate and kerogen type, so they are guides, not fixed rules. Vitrinite reflectance and Tmax track maturity.

Migration is primary (expulsion from the source), secondary (flow along carriers such as sands or faults) and tertiary (remigration or leakage after the trap, up to surface seepage). Buoyancy drives it; capillary pressure resists it.

sections.heading: Reservoir, seal and traps
sections.text:
A reservoir is porous and permeable rock, usually sandstone or carbonate, that stores oil or gas. Porosity is the pore fraction; permeability measures flow. A seal, or cap rock, is a low-permeability layer with high capillary entry pressure, commonly shale or salt.

A trap holds the hydrocarbons: structural traps include anticlines and fault blocks; stratigraphic traps include pinch-outs and reefs. A play is a family of prospects sharing source, reservoir and seal.

sections.heading: Modelling and workflows
sections.text:
Basin modelling reconstructs burial, temperature and maturity through time to predict generation and migration. It is calibrated with measured maturity and pressure data.

Exploration runs from basin screening to play mapping, seismic interpretation, prospect mapping and volumetric estimation. Appraisal then delineates the find with wells, cores and flow tests before development.

Volumetric oil in place: stock tank oil initially in place (STOIIP) = GRV × N/G × φ × (1 − Sw) ÷ Bo, where N/G is net-to-gross, φ porosity, Sw water saturation and Bo the formation volume factor (reservoir volume per stock tank volume). With gross rock volume (GRV) 10,000,000 m³, N/G 0.6, φ 0.25, Sw 0.3 and Bo 1.2: 10,000,000 × 0.6 × 0.25 × 0.7 ÷ 1.2 = 875,000 m³ of oil at surface (stock tank) conditions.

keyPoints: Kerogen Type I and II are oil-prone; Type III is gas-prone.
Oil and gas windows are approximate temperature ranges that vary with heating rate.
Migration moves hydrocarbons from source to trap by buoyancy.
A working petroleum system needs source, reservoir, seal, trap and correct timing.
STOIIP = GRV × N/G × φ × (1 − Sw) ÷ Bo.
Exploration identifies prospects; appraisal defines them before development.

en.title: Hydrogeology and groundwater
en.short: The water cycle, aquifers, Darcy’s law, pumping tests and groundwater contamination.

sections.heading: The water cycle and recharge
sections.text:
The hydrological cycle moves water between ocean, atmosphere and land by evaporation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and discharge. Recharge is water that reaches the saturated zone and adds to storage; discharge leaves it through springs, pumping, rivers or evapotranspiration.

Recharge is hard to measure, so it is estimated from water-table fluctuations, tracers or a water balance. It is often seasonal, and in arid regions it may be only a small fraction of rainfall.

sections.heading: Aquifers and their properties
sections.text:
An aquifer stores and transmits water in usable amounts; an aquitard transmits little. Unconfined aquifers have a water table at atmospheric pressure. Confined aquifers lie beneath a confining layer; their water is under pressure, so the level in a well rises above the aquifer top, along the piezometric surface.

Porosity is the fraction of void space. Permeability is the ease of flow, commonly measured as hydraulic conductivity: clay has high porosity but low permeability. Storativity is the volume released per unit area per unit fall in head; unconfined aquifers use specific yield, the fraction that drains by gravity, often 0.1 to 0.3.

sections.heading: Darcy’s law and wells
sections.text:
Darcy’s law: Q = K i A, where K is hydraulic conductivity, i the hydraulic gradient, the head drop per unit distance, and A the cross-sectional area. It applies to laminar flow. Transmissivity T = Kb, with b the saturated thickness.

Example: K = 10 m/day, i = 0.002, A = 50 m².
Q = 10 × 0.002 × 50 = 1 m³/day.
With b = 30 m, T = 10 × 30 = 300 m²/day.

Pumping tests measure drawdown, the fall in water level, with time; the Theis and Cooper-Jacob methods give T and S.

sections.heading: Chemistry, contamination and examples
sections.text:
Groundwater chemistry reflects the rocks it passes through and its residence time. Contamination comes from pit latrines and septic tanks, fertilisers, fuel spills, mine drainage and seawater intrusion in coastal wells. The vadose zone, the unsaturated material above the water table, and sound well construction give protection.

Examples: the sedimentary aquifers of Nigeria’s Sokoto, Chad and Benue basins; the weathered basement complex; the Nubian Sandstone aquifer of North Africa; the High Plains aquifer in the United States. Yields vary, so check local water-board data.

keyPoints: Recharge adds water to storage; discharge removes it.
Porosity is storage space; permeability is the ability to transmit water.
Darcy’s law: Q = K i A, and transmissivity T = Kb.
Storativity is the volume released per unit area per unit fall in head.
Theis and Cooper-Jacob analysis of pumping tests give transmissivity and storativity.
Contamination risk depends on the vadose zone, well construction and land use.

en.title: Engineering geology and geohazards
en.short: Rock and soil properties, rock mass classification, site investigation, geohazards and mitigation.

sections.heading: Materials and discontinuities
sections.text: Engineering geology applies geology to design and construction. Rock and soil are engineering materials, judged by strength, stiffness, permeability, durability and compressibility. Soil is a three-phase mixture of particles, water and air; its behaviour depends on grain size, density, water content and stress history. A rock mass is intact rock plus discontinuities such as joints, bedding and faults. These planes usually control deformation, permeability and failure, so intact strength alone can mislead.

sections.heading: Classification and investigation
sections.text: Rock mass classification turns observations into design numbers. The Rock Mass Rating (RMR) combines intact strength, rock quality designation (RQD), discontinuity spacing and condition, groundwater and orientation. The Q system uses RQD, joint set number, roughness, alteration, water and stress. The Geological Strength Index (GSI) estimates mass strength from blockiness and surface condition. Site investigation begins with desk study and walkover, then boreholes, trial pits, in situ tests, geophysics and laboratory tests. It must identify strata, groundwater, discontinuities and old workings.

sections.heading: Geohazards
sections.text: Landslides are downslope soil or rock movement under gravity, triggered by rain, excavation or earthquakes. Subsidence is ground lowering by collapse, dissolution, mining or fluid withdrawal. Earthquake hazards include shaking, liquefaction (loss of soil strength), landslides and fault rupture. Volcanic hazards include lava, ash, pyroclastic flows, lahars (volcanic mudflows) and gas. Hazard is the probability of a damaging event; risk combines hazard with exposure and vulnerability. Assessment uses mapping, monitoring and recurrence records. Mitigation may avoid the hazard, drain or support slopes, improve ground, enforce planning and building codes, or install warnings.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Factor of safety = resisting forces ÷ driving forces. With resisting force 180 kN and driving force 120 kN, FS = 1.5, so the slope is stable in that simple model. The 1966 Aberfan tip failure in Wales showed how ignored groundwater and spoil loading can cause catastrophic landslide. Illustrative case: a school on a clay slope above a village is moved after investigation finds old mine workings and seepage.

keyPoints: Rock mass behaviour depends on intact rock plus discontinuities such as joints, bedding and faults.
Soil engineering properties include strength, stiffness, permeability and compressibility.
RMR, Q and GSI are standard rock mass classifications used for support and design.
Site investigation moves from desk study and walkover to boreholes, in situ tests, geophysics and laboratory tests.
Hazard is the probability of an event; risk combines hazard with exposure and vulnerability.
Factor of safety = resisting forces ÷ driving forces, and Q = (RQD ÷ Jn) × (Jr ÷ Ja) × (Jw ÷ SRF).

en.title: Environmental geology and mining
en.short: Geological controls on contamination, mine waste, landfill siting, erosion, EIA and past climate records.

sections.heading: Contamination controls
sections.text: Contamination is governed by source, pathway and receptor. Geology controls the pathway: porosity and permeability set how fast water moves; clay and organic matter adsorb metals; pH and redox (oxidation state) decide whether elements dissolve or precipitate; faults, fractures and mine workings can form fast routes. A site investigation maps these features and samples soil, rock and water. The same spill may be harmless on a clay-rich site with a deep water table and serious on a permeable, fractured aquifer.

sections.heading: Mine waste and acid drainage
sections.text: Acid mine drainage (AMD) forms when sulfide minerals, mainly pyrite (FeS2), oxidise in air and water. The overall reaction is 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O gives 4Fe(OH)3 + 8SO4²− + 16H+. The acid dissolves metals and harms streams. Waste rock, tailings (fine waste from ore processing) and exposed pit walls are sources. Management uses encapsulation, water covers, alkaline neutralisation and treatment. Acid potential is compared with neutralisation capacity; both vary by deposit. Drainage can persist for decades.

sections.heading: Landfills and erosion
sections.text: Landfill siting avoids permeable rocks, active faults, floodplains and shallow water tables. A compacted clay liner and leachate collection (capturing contaminated water draining from waste) reduce escape; monitoring wells check performance. Land degradation by erosion removes fertile soil. Example: 10 t/ha/yr lost for 20 years is 200 t/ha. With bulk density 1.3 t/m³, thickness = 200 ÷ (10 × 1.3) = 15.4 mm. Rates vary with climate, slope, cover and land use.

sections.heading: EIA and past change
sections.text: Environmental impact assessment (EIA) predicts effects before a project, compares alternatives, and sets mitigation and monitoring. It needs baseline data and should treat cumulative and transboundary effects. Rocks and sediments archive past change: oxygen and carbon isotopes, pollen, grain size, varves (annual sediment layers) and fossils record temperature, rainfall and sea level. These archives show natural variability and help separate human impact from background. Interpretations carry uncertainty and need dating.

keyPoints: Contamination depends on source, pathway and receptor; permeability, fractures, pH and redox control movement.
Pyrite oxidation, 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O gives 4Fe(OH)3 + 8SO4²− + 16H+, produces acid and sulfate.
Landfill siting needs low-permeability geology, leachate collection and groundwater monitoring away from faults and floodplains.
Soil loss thickness (mm) = loss (t/ha) ÷ (10 × bulk density in t/m³).
EIA predicts impacts, compares alternatives and sets mitigation and monitoring.
Rocks and sediments record past climate through isotopes, pollen, grain size and fossils; dating and uncertainty matter.

en.title: Geological field mapping and exploration
en.short: Planning field mapping, sampling, drilling, core logging, remote sensing, GIS and reporting.

sections.heading: Planning the project
sections.text: Start with a clear aim and a study area small enough to finish. Choose a base map (a map for recording observations) and scale: at 1:10,000, 1 cm on the map is 100 m on the ground. Check access, landowner permission and permits, which vary by country. Prepare a safety plan, budget, equipment list and daily route. Reconnaissance visits help adjust the plan before full mapping.

sections.heading: Mapping and sampling
sections.text: Map by traverses (planned routes across the area) and outcrop stations (places where rock is exposed). Mark contacts, faults and folds on the base map and record strike and dip where relevant. Give each station coordinates and a unique number. Take representative, fresh samples, label them with location, date and orientation if needed, and keep a field notebook and a chain of custody (a record of who handled each sample). Sampling density depends on the question and the rock variability; state your rule.

sections.heading: Drilling and core logging
sections.text: Drilling recovers cylindrical rock core or broken cuttings. Log core at fixed intervals: lithology, contacts, structures, alteration, recovery and rock quality designation (RQD). Recovery = recovered length ÷ run length × 100. RQD = total length of core pieces 100 mm or longer ÷ run length × 100. Example: a 150 cm run recovers 140 cm, so recovery = 140 ÷ 150 × 100 = 93.3%. If pieces 100 mm or longer total 105 cm, RQD = 105 ÷ 150 × 100 = 70%.

sections.heading: Remote sensing, GIS and reporting
sections.text: Remote sensing uses satellite images, aerial photographs and digital elevation models (DEMs) to show linear features, landforms and access before fieldwork. A geographic information system (GIS) stores maps, coordinates and sample data as layers for query and map production. Field checking is still essential.
