Present results as a geological map, cross-sections, stratigraphic columns and tables. The report states aim, methods, results, interpretation, limitations and references, with data in appendices.

keyPoints: A field project starts with clear aims, a suitable base map and scale, permits, a safety plan and a budget.
Record every station and sample with coordinates, a unique number and enough field notes for another geologist to repeat the work.
Recovery = recovered core length ÷ drilled run length × 100.
RQD = total length of core pieces 100 mm or longer ÷ run length × 100.
Remote sensing and GIS help plan fieldwork and present layers, but field checking remains essential.
A report should include a geological map, cross-sections, methods, results, interpretation, limitations and references.

en.title: Professional practice and geoscience ethics
en.short: Professional bodies, codes of conduct, JORC and NI 43-101 reporting, safety and ethics.

sections.heading: Bodies and registration
sections.text:
A professional body sets standards; a statutory regulator is created by law and can require registration. The Council of Nigerian Mining Engineers and Geoscientists (COMEG) is Nigeria’s statutory regulator: it registers geoscientists and mining engineers and can discipline them.

The Geological Society of London is a learned society and professional body in the United Kingdom. It awards the title Chartered Geologist (CGeol), requires a code of conduct and continuing professional development (CPD), but is not a statutory regulator.

Examples elsewhere include AIPG in the United States and AIG in Australia. Rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Codes of conduct
sections.text:
A code of conduct is a set of rules and ethical standards that a professional body requires members to follow. It usually covers honesty, competence, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, safety, respect for the environment and local communities, and accurate records.

A geologist should sign only work within their competence, disclose limits and uncertainties, and keep skills current through CPD. Breaches can lead to suspension or removal from the register.

sections.heading: Reporting standards
sections.text:
Public reporting of mineral projects follows standards such as the JORC Code (Australia) and NI 43-101 (Canada). They require transparency, materiality and competence.

A Mineral Resource is a concentration of material with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction. A Mineral Reserve is the economically mineable part of a Measured or Indicated Resource.

JORC uses a Competent Person; NI 43-101 uses a Qualified Person. Both must have relevant experience and be accountable for the statement. Inferred Resources cannot be reported as Reserves.

sections.heading: Safety and responsibility
sections.text:
Health and safety begins with risk assessment: identify hazards, estimate likelihood and severity, and apply controls. Use PPE, follow site inductions and emergency plans, and report incidents. Legal duties vary by country.

Public responsibility means communicating uncertainty honestly, protecting communities and the environment, and refusing to mislead. Case: Ama, a COMEG-registered geologist in Nigeria, is asked to call Inferred Resources 'reserves’ in a press release. She refuses, cites JORC and NI 43-101, and records her advice.

keyPoints: COMEG is Nigeria’s statutory regulator for geoscientists and mining engineers; the Geological Society of London is a UK professional body that awards Chartered Geologist status.
A code of conduct requires honesty, competence, confidentiality, safety and respect for communities and the environment.
JORC (Australia) and NI 43-101 (Canada) set minimum standards for public reporting of exploration results, mineral resources and reserves.
A Mineral Resource is not a Mineral Reserve; Inferred Resources cannot be reported as Reserves.
JORC requires a Competent Person and NI 43-101 requires a Qualified Person, each accountable for the public statement.
Health and safety starts with risk assessment, and public responsibility means reporting uncertainty honestly and refusing to mislead.

en.title: Advanced tectonics and geodynamics
en.short: Driving forces, mantle flow, lithospheric deformation, rift to collision systems and tectonics-sedimentation links.

sections.heading: Driving forces and mantle flow
sections.text: Plate motion is driven mainly by slab pull, the negative buoyancy of cold subducting lithosphere. Ridge push from elevated mid-ocean ridges is smaller; basal drag from mantle flow can either drive or resist. Mantle convection is often treated as whole-mantle or layered; plumes are narrow upwellings. The Rayleigh number Ra = ρgαΔTd³/(κη) measures convection vigour, where ρ is density, g gravity, α thermal expansivity, ΔT temperature contrast, d layer depth, κ thermal diffusivity and η viscosity. High Ra means vigorous flow. Values vary, so use source-specific parameters.

sections.heading: Extension and passive margins
sections.text: Lithospheric deformation is elastic, brittle or ductile depending on temperature, composition and strain rate. Rifting stretches and thins the lithosphere, producing normal faults, basins and eventual breakup. A passive margin forms after breakup; it subsides thermally and accumulates a sediment wedge. Strain rate = velocity ÷ length. Example: a 1000 km wide rift extends at 50 mm per year. Convert to metres: 0.05 m per year ÷ 1,000,000 m = 0.00000005 per year, or 5 × 10^-8 per year. Over 1 million years the extension is 0.05, or 5%.

sections.heading: Subduction, collision and orogeny
sections.text: Subduction consumes lithosphere; slab dip, rollback and sediment supply control arc and wedge growth. Collision thickens crust by thrusting and folding, causing metamorphism, uplift and exhumation. Orogens balance shortening against erosion and isostasy. Orogenic processes include accretion, underplating, plateau growth and collapse. The style depends on convergence rate, crustal strength and inherited structure.

sections.heading: Tectonics and sedimentation
sections.text: Tectonics sets accommodation, sediment supply and stratal geometry. Syn-tectonic growth strata record deposition during faulting, thickening toward active normal faults and thinning over growing folds; unconformities mark uplift or starvation. Source-to-sink analysis links hinterland exhumation to basin fill. Quantitative tectonic analysis uses strain rates, balanced cross-sections, flexural models, subsidence curves and thermochronology. Always state assumptions and uncertainties; results differ by method and data.

keyPoints: Slab pull is generally the largest plate driving force; ridge push is smaller, and basal drag can drive or resist.
Mantle convection vigour is measured by Ra = ρgαΔTd³/(κη), where η is dynamic viscosity.
Strain rate = velocity ÷ length; 50 mm per year across 1000 km gives 5 × 10^-8 per year, or 5% in 1 million years.
Rifts and passive margins record extension, thinning and thermal subsidence; subduction and collision record convergence, thickening and exhumation.
Tectonics controls accommodation, sediment supply and stratal geometry; growth strata record deposition during faulting.
Quantitative tectonic analysis uses strain rates, balanced sections, flexure and thermochronology, and must state its assumptions.

en.title: Advanced basin analysis and petroleum systems
en.short: Basin types, subsidence, sequence stratigraphy, petroleum systems, play risk and basin modelling.

sections.heading: Basin types
sections.text:
A sedimentary basin is a long-lived depression filled with sediment. Advanced classification links basin geometry and subsidence to plate setting. Rift basins form by extension and crustal thinning. Passive margins follow rifting and then thermal cooling. Foreland basins form by flexure under thrust loads. Forearc and backarc basins lie at convergent margins. Intracratonic sag basins and pull-apart basins at strike-slip bends are other types.

Subsidence mechanisms include crustal thinning, thermal contraction, flexural loading, sediment loading and compaction. Backstripping removes sediment load and compaction to estimate tectonic subsidence.

sections.heading: Sequence stratigraphy
sections.text:
At basin scale, sequence stratigraphy divides the fill into sequences bounded by unconformities or correlative conformities. Accommodation is the space available for sediment. It is set by subsidence plus eustatic (global) sea-level change. Sediment supply fills that space.

The balance between accommodation and supply produces systems tracts, such as lowstand, transgressive and highstand tracts. Seismic reflection, well logs and biostratigraphy are correlated to map these units across the basin.

sections.heading: Petroleum system
sections.text:
A petroleum system requires source rock, reservoir, seal, trap and migration path. Processes are generation, expulsion, migration, accumulation and preservation. Timing is critical: the trap must exist before hydrocarbon migration.

Basin modelling reconstructs burial history, temperature and source-rock maturity. It tests whether generation and migration could fill the trap. The model is calibrated with measured maturity, pressure and thermal data.

sections.heading: Play and risk
sections.text:
A play is a family of prospects sharing source, reservoir, seal and trap. Prospect evaluation estimates recoverable volume and chance of success. Independent geological chances are multiplied. Dependent risks are not simply multiplied.

Expected monetary value is EMV = P(success) × NPV(success) − P(failure) × dry-hole cost, where NPV is net present value. Example: P(success) = 0.25, NPV = $80 million, dry-hole cost = $10 million. EMV = 0.25 × 80 − 0.75 × 10 = 20 − 7.5 = $12.5 million. Monte Carlo simulation and sensitivity analysis show which uncertainties matter most.

keyPoints: Basin classification links subsidence and geometry to plate setting.
Backstripping separates tectonic subsidence from sediment and compaction effects.
Accommodation is subsidence plus eustatic change; the balance of accommodation and sediment supply sets systems tracts.
A petroleum system needs source, reservoir, seal, trap, migration and correct timing.
Prospect chance of success is the product of independent geological chances.
EMV = P(success) × NPV(success) − P(failure) × dry-hole cost.

en.title: Geological modelling and geostatistics
en.short: 3D geological models, variograms, kriging, simulation, uncertainty, resource estimation and machine learning.

sections.heading: 3D geological modelling
sections.text: A three-dimensional geological model is a computer representation of rock volumes, boundaries and properties. It is built from drill holes, geological maps, geophysics and interpreted cross-sections. An explicit model stores surfaces and volumes directly; an implicit model uses mathematical functions to interpolate boundaries. Models are held in a grid or block model, whose cells carry lithology, grade or other properties. Scale and data support matter: a model is only as good as its inputs and its geological assumptions.

sections.heading: Variograms and kriging
sections.text: Geostatistics uses spatial correlation. The variogram measures how quickly values differ with distance. For lag h, γ(h) = 1 ÷ (2N) Σ [z(xi) − z(xi+h)]², where N is the number of pairs. A model variogram has a nugget (noise), a sill (variance) and a range (distance beyond which values are uncorrelated). Kriging is a weighted average that uses this model. Ordinary kriging weights sum to one and give an estimate plus a kriging variance. Example: values 2, 4 and 5 at unit spacing give differences (2−4)² = 4 and (4−5)² = 1, so γ(1) = (4+1) ÷ (2×2) = 1.25.

sections.heading: Simulation and uncertainty
sections.text: Kriging smooths grades and underestimates variability. Conditional simulation produces equally probable realisations that honour the data and variogram. Their spread measures uncertainty. Resource estimation uses a block model, cut-off grade and grade-tonnage curve to report tonnage and contained metal. Classification into measured, indicated and inferred resources depends on data density and confidence; the rules differ by country and reporting code. Machine learning methods such as random forests and neural networks can predict grade or lithology, but need separate training, validation and test data to avoid overfitting.

sections.heading: Validation and reporting
sections.text: Validate a model by cross-validation, visual checks against drill holes, geological plausibility and sensitivity tests. Report data sources, assumptions, software, variogram parameters, search ellipses and limitations. Public reporting follows codes such as the JORC Code in Australia and NI 43-101 in Canada, and needs a qualified or competent person. A model is an interpretation, not a fact; uncertainty should be stated plainly.

keyPoints: 3D geological models combine drill holes, maps, geophysics and interpretation in a grid or block model.
The experimental variogram is γ(h) = 1 ÷ (2N) Σ [z(xi) − z(xi+h)]², with nugget, sill and range describing the model variogram.
Ordinary kriging is a weighted average with weights summing to one; it gives an estimate and a kriging variance.
Conditional simulation gives multiple realisations for uncertainty, while kriging alone smooths values.
Resource estimates depend on cut-off grade, data density and reporting codes, which vary by country.
Validate models by cross-validation, geological plausibility and sensitivity, report assumptions and limitations, and test machine learning on independent data.

en.title: Research methods and thesis design
en.short: Research questions, literature review, sampling and data quality, methods, ethics, and writing and defending a thesis.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question is the focused uncertainty your thesis answers. It must be answerable with your time, data and equipment, and it must matter. Test it in one sentence: in this area, how does this process vary with this factor? Narrow a broad topic into something you can finish. A hypothesis is a testable prediction; a question is open, a hypothesis states the answer you expect.

sections.heading: Literature and sampling
sections.text: The literature review is a critical survey of published work. It shows what is known, what is contested and the gap your question fills. Group by idea, compare methods, cite primary sources. Sampling design is the plan for choosing which rocks, sites or people to study. Define the population, then sample randomly or in strata (subgroups) to reduce bias. Data quality means accuracy (closeness to the true value) and precision (repeatability). Calibrate instruments, run duplicates and blanks, and record location, date and method for every sample.

sections.heading: Methods and ethics
sections.text: Quantitative methods measure and count: geochemical assays, geophysical readings, statistical tests. Qualitative methods interpret meaning and context: interviews with miners, land-use histories, field observations. Many theses mix both. For example, a student studying well salinity could sample wells by depth and distance, then interview drillers about pumping. Ethics covers honest data and authorship, informed consent, site permission, field safety, and care for communities and the environment. Report data that contradict you; never hide them.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: Write as you work. Structure the thesis as introduction and question, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion. Every figure needs a caption that stands alone. In the defence (viva), you present briefly and answer examiners’ questions. Expect questions on why you chose your methods and what your data cannot show. Prepare by rereading your chapters and rehearsing short answers.

keyPoints: A good research question is focused, answerable and worth answering.
The literature review must identify the gap your question fills, not just summarise papers.
Sampling design controls bias; state the population and the selection method.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability.
Quantitative and qualitative methods answer different questions and are often combined.
Ethics requires honest reporting, consent, permission and field safety.
